source.title: When Does Monolingual Data Help Multilingual Translation: The Role of Domain and Model Scale
source.authors: Christos Baziotis; Biao Zhang; Alexandra Birch; B. Haddow

page_placements.theme: Descriptive improvements across modalities do not establish a shared predictive law

record.tranche_reason: It measures translation-task scores across model sizes, bearing on scale-related task performance, but uses neither held-out language-model cross-entropy nor the original scaling-law fits.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly says it does not study scaling laws. Its scale experiments report translation metrics for 90M, 370M and 1.6B MMT models; they do not test held-out pretraining loss, token or compute scaling laws, extrapolation from smaller runs, fixed-compute allocation, or architecture variation at a fixed parameter count. The cited scaling-law results are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It trains supervised encoder-decoder multilingual translation (MMT) models from scratch at three sizes (90M, 370M, 1.6B) and asks how scale changes the benefit of backtranslation (BT) and denoising autoencoding (MASS). It reports no held-out pretraining loss and fits no power law. Nothing is extrapolated or forecast. Translation is the models' training task, not a downstream task of a pretrained language model. The authors state their work 'does not study scaling laws'. The recorded rows compare each method with the same-scale parallel-only model, so they measure a method effect, not a scale effect. The monotonic BLEU rise across three sizes is a related but different construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The headline finding is that BT and DAE are brittle to domain mismatch, especially at small scale. BT is best in-domain but can hurt out-of-domain and in low-resource directions, and DAE is less effective than earlier work reported (MASS beats BART). Scale matters most for DAE: MASS hurts at 90M and becomes comparable to or better than BT at 1.6B, especially in low-resource directions. The authors state they do not study scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than fitting held-out language-model loss against parameters, tokens or compute, the paper varies MMT model size and evaluates translation quality while comparing parallel-only, backtranslation and denoising-autoencoding training. Models are trained from scratch; it does not fit power laws or optimize compute allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Scale changes the effectiveness of MASS and BT; the paper also reports dependence on test/monolingual domain and resource level. BLEU, chrF and COMET do not always agree on the magnitude of scale effects.

fits_no_version.finding: Parallel-only MMT mean BLEU rises monotonically from 90M to 370M to 1.6B on all four test sets: ML50 20.6/22.9/25.4, FLORES 16.8/19.4/21.0, NTREX 15.5/17.8/19.4, TICO-19 19.7/22.3/24.1. chrF and COMET agree. Only three points; no fit or forecast.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Supervised multilingual translation quality improves monotonically with model size (90M–1.6B), without a fitted predictive law.

fits_no_version.finding: Gains from monolingual data grow with scale. MASS goes from below or equal to baseline at 90M (ML50 19.9 vs 20.6) to +1.3 BLEU at 1.6B, matching BT on ML50.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model capacity determines whether auxiliary monolingual objectives (DAE/BT) help supervised MMT.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (2023)
record.problems: The scale study uses three model sizes (90M, 370M and 1.6B) on one multilingual dataset and an English-centric setting. It reports translation metrics rather than held-out pretraining loss, and does not fit or validate a predictive law. The text notes possible non-generalization to other datasets, language settings and larger scales. Error bars are shown as standard errors of the mean in figures; uncertainty is not given for the tabulated means.
record.rows_left_out: Not extracted: per-language and resource-group scores, mixed-domain monolingual-data comparisons, BART-versus-MASS comparisons, and additional chrF/COMET results. These are outside the scale-mean BLEU rows retained for V6; see §5.1–5.3, Appendix Tables 4–11 and Figures 8–10. The scale figures and Tables 12–15 also report additional metric and disaggregated results not retained.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No shape comparison at a fixed parameter count; sizes differ in depth and width together.
Supervised MT is not analysed for a power-law form.
No pretrained language model with downstream evaluation. Translation scores at three sizes come with no fit, forecast or loss-to-metric relation.
No fitted exponents and no fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'supports V6' label is removed. The rows compare methods at the same scale rather than measuring scale. The study's models are supervised MT systems, not pretrained language models evaluated downstream. Three size points with no fit cannot show 'predictable' improvement. Model sizes also change training steps and batch size together (Table 3).

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy power laws in parameter count, tokens or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on small runs.
Fixed-compute loss-minimising parameter/token allocation and its trend.
Architecture comparisons at a fixed parameter count.
Power-law behaviour in other modalities or training regimes.

The study measures translation quality across model scale, but does not test downstream performance as a function of held-out pretraining loss, or forecast performance on new runs from a fitted relationship.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal allocations, fitting choices, or departures from single power-law curves.

relation.reason: Section 2 discusses scaling-law research and explicitly distinguishes its own model-capacity analysis from studying scaling laws.

tranche.reason: The study compares translation quality and the benefits of monolingual training methods across three model sizes. It neither tests nor uses a scaling law; these trends alone do not establish V6 predictability.

source_check.notes: All listed values are parallel-only controls, so cannot_determine is appropriate with no linked claim version. Tables 12–15 are in Appendix B.3 and support the scale analysis in §5.4; no fitted law or forecast is reported.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested MMT translation systems and test sets; 90M to 1.6B parameters
reader_labels.reason: Mean BLEU rises across the tested sizes for parallel-only, MASS and BT models on ML50, FLORES, NTREX and TICO-19 (r1–r36); this is evidence of scale-related task-score improvement, not an evaluated forecasting law.
